new_entities.name: Chronic stress with elevated cortisol burden
new_entities.description: Persistent psychological or physiological stress states characterized by higher cortisol exposure.

new_entities.name: Testosterone status in men
new_entities.description: Circulating testosterone level or testosterone-linked androgen status in men.

edges.effect_quant: The Caerphilly cohort found a higher morning cortisol:testosterone ratio predicted later ischemic heart disease with an age-adjusted odds ratio of 1.22 per standard-deviation increase, showing that chronic cortisol-dominant hormonal tone tracks with lower-androgen physiology rather than resilience. Smaller SABPA data then linked chronic distress and cortisol burden specifically to the low-testosterone male subgroup.
edges.population: adult men exposed to chronic psychological or physiological stress, including community cohorts and endurance-trained men with chronic energy stress
edges.mechanism: Persistent HPA-axis activation can suppress gonadotropin signalling and shift steroidogenesis toward cortisol-dominant physiology, especially when stress is paired with energy deficit, poor sleep, or cardiometabolic strain.
edges.summary: The literature supports a cautious harmful reading rather than dramatic certainty: chronic cortisol-heavy stress states in men are associated with lower-testosterone physiology, but the human evidence base is still built on a few cohorts and mechanistic reviews rather than large intervention trials.
edges.caveats: This edge is not strong enough to claim that every stressed man will show clinically low testosterone, and some of the evidence uses cortisol:testosterone balance or low-testosterone subgroups rather than clean before-and-after stress interventions.

evidence.notes: Cortisol, testosterone, and coronary heart disease: prospective evidence from the Caerphilly study.

effect_quant.comparator: incident ischemic heart disease per standard-deviation increase in cortisol:testosterone ratio

evidence.citation: MalanNT et al 2014 J Hum Hypertens
